name: Water
where: Every glass you drink, every cloud, and about 60 % of you.
why: Oxygen shares a pair of electrons with each hydrogen, and its other electrons push the two hydrogens into a bent shape.

name: Table salt
where: On food, and dissolved in your blood, your sweat and the sea.
why: Sodium hands one electron to chlorine; the two end up with opposite charges, and opposite charges cling.
note: There is no single salt molecule: sodium and chloride ions (charged atoms) stack into a cube, millions at a time.

name: Carbon dioxide
where: In every breath you breathe out, and in the bubbles of a fizzy drink.
why: Carbon shares two pairs of electrons with each oxygen (a double bond), so the three atoms sit in a straight line.

name: Oxygen gas
where: About a fifth of the air: the part your lungs are after.
why: An oxygen atom is two electrons short of a full outer shell, so two of them share two pairs and both are satisfied.
note: An element can pair with itself: the oxygen you breathe is two oxygen atoms bonded together.

name: Nitrogen gas
where: About four fifths of every breath, passing in and out unused.
why: Two nitrogens share three pairs of electrons (a triple bond), one of the strongest bonds there is, so the gas barely reacts.

name: Glucose
where: The sugar in your blood, made by plants from sunlight, and the fuel your cells burn.
why: Carbon atoms share electrons in a ring with one oxygen, and the hydrogens and other oxygens hang off its sides.

name: Sugar (sucrose)
where: The white sugar in the bowl, pressed from sugar cane or beet.
why: Two smaller sugar rings, glucose and fructose, are joined through a shared oxygen atom.

name: Methane
where: The gas that burns on a gas stove, and what cows and swamps give off.
why: Carbon shares one pair of electrons with each of four hydrogens, which spread out as far apart as they can, like a tripod with a mast.

name: Calcium carbonate
where: Eggshells, seashells, chalk, limestone and marble.
why: Calcium hands two electrons to a carbonate group (one carbon sharing electrons with three oxygens), and the charges cling.
note: It forms a crystal, not single molecules: calcium ions and carbonate groups stack in a repeating pattern.

name: Quartz
where: Most of the sand on a beach, and the raw stuff of glass.
why: Each silicon shares electrons with four oxygens, and each oxygen bridges two silicons, so the whole crystal is one web.
note: There is no single SiO₂ molecule: the bonds go on in every direction, which is why quartz is so hard.

name: Rust
where: On old bikes and nails, and the red in red soil and on Mars.
why: Forms when iron meets water and air over time: iron hands electrons to oxygen, and the charged atoms pack into a crystal.
note: Two iron to three oxygen is the ratio in which the charges balance.

name: Ethanol
where: The alcohol in wine and beer, made by yeast eating sugar.
why: Two carbons share a bond, and the oxygen sits at one end holding a hydrogen, which lets it mix with water.
note: Same atoms, different shape: dimethyl ether is also C₂H₆O, with the oxygen in the middle, and it is a gas.

name: Acetic acid (vinegar)
where: What makes vinegar sour: about 5 % of it, the rest is water.
why: Two carbons share a bond; one holds two oxygens, and the hydrogen on one of them comes away easily in water, which is what makes it an acid.

name: Baking soda
where: In cakes and bread, where it gives off carbon dioxide bubbles when it meets an acid.
why: Sodium hands one electron to a bicarbonate group (carbon, oxygen and hydrogen sharing electrons), and the charges cling.
note: A crystal of sodium ions and bicarbonate groups, not single molecules.

name: Caffeine
where: In coffee, tea and chocolate, where plants make it to put off insects.
why: Carbon and nitrogen atoms share electrons in two joined rings, with oxygens and small carbon groups on the edges.

name: Citric acid
where: The sour in lemons and limes.
why: A short carbon chain shares electrons with three acid groups, each with a hydrogen that comes away in water.

name: Ammonia
where: The sharp smell in some glass cleaners, and the start of most fertiliser.
why: Nitrogen shares one pair of electrons with each of three hydrogens; its spare pair pushes them into a low pyramid.

name: Bleach (sodium hypochlorite)
where: Household bleach: a few percent of it dissolved in water.
why: Sodium hands one electron to a hypochlorite group (chlorine sharing electrons with oxygen), which grabs electrons from stains and germs.
note: As a solid it is a crystal of ions (charged atoms); you meet it dissolved.

name: Hydrogen gas
where: The lightest gas; most of the Sun, and a fuel that burns to plain water.
why: Each hydrogen has one electron; two of them share their electrons as a pair, and both are satisfied.
note: An element can pair with itself: hydrogen gas is two hydrogen atoms bonded together.

name: Argon
where: Nearly 1 % of the air you breathe, passing through untouched.
why: Its outer shell of electrons is already full, so it has nothing to share or hand over.
note: Argon stays on its own: noble gases (the last column) almost never combine.

name: Ozone
where: High in the sky, where a thin layer of it blocks most of the Sun's harshest light.
why: Three oxygens share electrons in a bent chain; the bonds are strained, so ozone breaks apart easily.
note: The same element, a different count: three oxygens make ozone, two make the oxygen you breathe.

name: Lactic acid
where: In working muscles, and the tang in yoghurt and sourdough.
why: A three-carbon chain shares electrons with an acid group at one end, whose hydrogen comes away in water.

name: Urea
where: How your body gets rid of spare nitrogen, in urine; also a farm fertiliser.
why: One carbon shares a double bond with oxygen and single bonds with two nitrogens, each holding two hydrogens.
note: The first body chemical made in a lab (1828), which showed life's molecules follow the same rules as everything else.

name: Glycine
where: The simplest amino acid: a building block of every protein in you.
why: Two carbons share a bond; one carries a nitrogen group, the other an acid group, and those ends link amino acids into chains.

name: Adenine
where: The "A" of DNA's four letters, in every cell you have.
why: Carbons and nitrogens share electrons in two joined rings, flat like a tile, which lets it stack inside DNA.

name: Calcium phosphate
where: The hard part of your bones and teeth.
why: Calcium hands electrons to phosphate groups (phosphorus sharing electrons with four oxygens), and the charges lock into a crystal.
note: Three calcium to two phosphate is the ratio in which the charges balance. Bone builds it on a mesh of protein.

name: Quicklime
where: Made by roasting limestone; the start of cement and mortar.
why: Calcium hands two electrons to oxygen, and the two charged atoms stack like table salt.
note: A crystal of calcium and oxide ions (charged atoms), with the same cube pattern as table salt.

name: Titanium dioxide
where: The bright white in most paint, toothpaste and mineral sunscreen.
why: Titanium hands electrons to two oxygens, and the charged atoms pack tightly into a crystal that scatters light.
note: A crystal, not single molecules.

name: Corundum
where: Ruby and sapphire are this, coloured by a trace of another metal; and the same oxide forms the thin skin on aluminium foil.
why: Aluminium hands electrons to oxygen, and the tightly packed charged atoms make one of the hardest minerals.
note: Two aluminium to three oxygen is the ratio in which the charges balance.

name: Magnetite
where: A black iron ore that is naturally magnetic: the first compasses used it.
why: Iron hands electrons to oxygen in two different amounts, two or three each, and the mix packs into a magnetic crystal.
note: Like rust, but with less oxygen: three iron to four oxygen.

name: Pyrite (fool's gold)
where: Shiny gold-coloured cubes in rock, called fool's gold.
why: Iron hands electrons to pairs of sulfur atoms, which share electrons with each other, and the crystal grows as cubes.
note: The cube-shaped crystals you can find in rock are the lattice, grown large.

name: Hydrogen sulfide
where: The rotten-egg smell of volcanoes and hot springs.
why: Like water, with sulfur in oxygen's place: sulfur shares a pair of electrons with each hydrogen, in a bent shape.

name: Steel
where: Bridges, cars, rails, knives: the most used metal there is.
why: Iron atoms share a sea of loose electrons; small carbon atoms tucked between them stop the layers sliding, so it is much harder than iron.
note: Steel has no fixed formula: it is iron with up to about 2 % carbon. A mix of metals like this is an alloy, not a compound.

name: Bronze
where: Statues, bells and medals; the first alloy people made, about 5,000 years ago.
why: Copper and tin atoms share a sea of loose electrons; the bigger tin atoms jam the layers, so bronze is harder than either.
note: Bronze has no fixed formula: usually about nine parts copper to one of tin. An alloy is a mix, not a compound.

name: Dimethyl ether
where: A gas used to push the spray out of some aerosol cans.
why: The oxygen sits between two carbons and holds no hydrogen of its own, so unlike ethanol it boils away below freezing.
note: Same atoms, different shape: ethanol is also C₂H₆O, with the oxygen at the end, and it is a liquid.

name: Hydrogen peroxide
where: A mild bleach and disinfectant, fizzing on a cut.
why: Water with one more oxygen: two oxygens share a weak bond, which breaks easily and gives off oxygen.

name: Carbon monoxide
where: From fires and engines that burn without enough air; poisonous and without smell.
why: Carbon and oxygen share three pairs of electrons; it clings to your blood more tightly than oxygen does.

name: Nitrogen dioxide
where: The brown haze of city smog, from hot engines.
why: Nitrogen shares electrons with two oxygens but is left with one unpaired electron, which makes it eager to react.

name: Chlorine gas
where: A yellow-green gas used to keep pools and tap water free of germs.
why: Each chlorine is one electron short of a full outer shell, so two of them share one pair.
note: An element can pair with itself: chlorine gas is two chlorine atoms bonded together.

name: Sulfuric acid
where: In car batteries, and the most made chemical in industry.
why: Sulfur shares electrons with four oxygens; two of them hold hydrogens that come away in water, which makes it a strong acid.
